name: BQ51050BRHLR
title: Qi v1.2 wireless receiver with integrated single-cell Li-ion charger
summary: The bq51050B, bq51051B and bq51052B take power from a Qi transmitter through a receiver coil and charge a single Li-ion or Li-polymer cell directly, to 4.20 V, 4.35 V or 4.40 V. One chip holds the synchronous rectifier, an LDO charge regulator, the Qi v1.2 digital controller and the charge logic, with NTC (JEITA) monitoring. The rectifier voltage tracks just above the battery to keep efficiency high, and an AD input hands charging over to a wired charger.
key_figures: 500 to 1500 mA (bq51050B/51B), 500 to 1000 mA (bq51052B), set by RILIM
4 to 10 V operating at RECT; AC1/AC2 rated -0.8 to 20 V

circuits.title: Wireless receiver charging a 4.2-V Li-ion cell at 800 mA
circuits.description: The receiver coil with C1 in series and C2 across the AC pins forms the dual resonant tank for Qi. CBOOT, CCOMM and CCLAMP sit between each AC pin and its BOOT, COMM and CLAMP pin. RECT is filtered by C3 and feeds the FOD node through ROS. R1 plus RFOD (393 Ω total) on ILIM gives 800 mA of charge current, and R5 (2.4 kΩ) on TERM ends the charge at 80 mA. BAT, decoupled by C4, charges the pack, whose 10 kΩ NTC sits on TS/CTRL; the host can also drive TS/CTRL with a three-state line and EN2 with a two-state line. D1 and R4 from BAT to CHG light while charging. AD is tied to PGND and AD-EN is left open.

circuits.title: Wireless receiver with a wired charger on a USB or adapter input
circuits.description: The wireless side is the 800 mA design unchanged. An adapter or USB input, bypassed by C5, drives AD and reaches a bq24040 wired charger through Q1, a back-to-back pair of P-channel FETs whose gates AD-EN drives, so neither source can feed the other. When AD rises above VAD-Pres the bq5105xB turns BAT off and AD-EN turns Q1 on; the bq24040 then charges the same pack from its OUT pin. Its ISET and PRETERM resistors, LEDs on /PG and /CHG, and C6, C7 follow the bq24040 data sheet. The pack thermistor goes to the bq24040 TS pin, the host drives TS/CTRL, EN2 and ISET2.

circuits.title: Capacitive load modulation
circuits.description: One capacitor runs from each COMM pin to its AC pin. With both switches closed the two 47 nF parts in series put about 22 nF across the coil, which the transmitter sees as a change in coil current.

circuits.title: Resistive load modulation
circuits.description: A 24 Ω resistor from the rectifier output to each COMM pin. One COMM pin handles a resistor of 24 Ω at most; for 12 Ω to 24 Ω the two COMM pins are paralleled, and below 12 Ω is not supported.

circuits.title: NTC network with series and parallel resistors
circuits.description: TS/CTRL is pulled up inside to VTSB through about 20 kΩ (R2 in the equations). Outside, R1 in series with the NTC runs to ground, R3 lies across that string, and C3 filters the pin. R1 and R3 are found from the two threshold equations at the chosen cold and hot temperatures.

circuits.title: NTC network with a series resistor only
circuits.description: The same pin with only R1 in series with the NTC to ground and C3 as filter; R3 is left out.

operation.text: A Qi charging pad and the receiver each carry a coil; set on the pad they couple like a loose transformer, and the pad sets the power level by moving its drive frequency. The receiver talks back by switching a load across its coil, which shows up as a change in the pad's coil current. Packets are digital, differential bi-phase coded at 2 kbps, and include identification and authentication, error, control, power usage, end-of-power and efficiency packets. The pad sleeps and pings now and then; it stays on only while a receiver identifies itself, and from then on the receiver controls the transfer.

The bq5105xB measures RECT, compares it with its target and sends control error packets until RECT settles. Its LDO stays off until RECT reaches VRECT-REG; then the voltage loop holds BAT at the regulation voltage. Error packets go out every 250 ms, or every 32 ms after a large transient. RECT is kept just above the battery so little voltage drops across the LDO.

The transmitter starts with an extended digital ping. The receiver answers with its signal-strength, then configuration and identification packets; once these arrive it holds a power contract and steers the operating point. A shutdown condition on EN2, AD or TS/CTRL makes it send an end-power-transfer packet right away instead. Under Dynamic Rectifier Control the receiver first raises RECT above 5 V and only then turns its output on, which helps the start-up transient.

In the main loop the rectifier target follows the charge state: VRECT-REG below VLOWV, VBAT + VTRACK while the current is above KPRECHG of IBULK, and VRECT-REG again at low current. The loop also measures rectified power, reports it, and checks the shutdown conditions. The Qi loop is slow, taking up to 90 ms to reach a new target, so the instant response to a load step is open loop and set by the coil's output impedance.

Three phases: precharge, constant-current fast charge and constant voltage. Above VLOWV and through most of the taper RECT tracks VBAT + VTRACK; below VLOWV it rises to VRECT-REG. When IBAT drops under IEndTrack in taper (35 % of IBULK on bq51050B/51B, 5 % on bq51052B) RECT goes back to VRECT-REG.

At VBAT ≤ VLOWV the current is limited to IPRECHG, KPRECHG (20 % typ) of IBULK; 800 mA of IBULK gives 160 mA. Below VBAT(SC) the part sources only IBAT(SC) until the cell climbs past VBAT(SC). Precharge is normally a small part of the whole charge.

operation.topic: Fast charge, constant voltage and termination
operation.text: Above VLOWV the pass MOSFETs from RECT to BAT hold the current at IBULK. At the regulation voltage the part holds BAT at VOREG and the current falls. When IBAT drops under ITERM-Th it sends EPT Charge Complete and its output goes high impedance.
Leaving TERM open disables termination. Grounding TERM also effectively disables it, though comparator offsets can still end the charge at very low current.

Charging starts only with VTS between the T1 (0 °C) and T4 (60 °C) thresholds; outside them charging pauses until the temperature returns. Between T1 and T2 (10 °C) and between T3 (45 °C) and T4 the current halves to IBULK/2. From T1 to T3 the voltage is VOREG; from T3 to T4 it drops to VO-J.
The current stays at IBULK across the whole T1 to T4 window; only the voltage changes, falling to VO-J between T3 and T4.

If RECT jumps, for example when the receiver shifts on the pad, the voltage loop keeps BAT from passing its regulation level and error packets go out every 32 ms until RECT is back, then every 250 ms. Above VOVP the internal FET opens, the receiver asks the transmitter to bring RECT back to VRECT-REG, and CLAMP1/CLAMP2 switch their capacitors in to keep the part below its ratings.
CHG is an open-drain NMOS rated to 20 V, on whenever BAT is enabled. The output is not enabled while RECT fails to reach its no-load target.

Two identical FETs on COMM1 and COMM2 modulate the receiver load. Capacitive modulation is the more usual choice: with capacitors from COMM1 to AC1 and COMM2 to AC2, closing the switches puts about 22 nF across the AC pins. For resistive modulation each COMM pin takes at most a 24 Ω resistor; 12 Ω to 24 Ω needs both pins in parallel, and less than 12 Ω is not supported.

A load step looks to the transmitter like a communication pulse, so during packets the regulator’s current limit is adjusted to keep load transients off the coil; the output load is held at 400 mA while packets are sent.

The rectifier is an all-NMOS H-bridge whose body diodes rectify while it is off. At start-up the diodes alone supply RECT. Above VUVLO it runs half-synchronous; above IBAT-SR it goes fully synchronous and stays so until the load falls below the IBAT-SRH hysteresis.

TS/CTRL compares the voltage of a battery NTC network, as a fraction of VTSB, with hot and cold thresholds; any NTC can be fitted to them with R1 and, if needed, R3. The bias is applied only while a TS reading is taken, for about 25 ms in each communication period of typically 240 ms; every comparator is deglitched for 10 ms. With the bias off the pin is high impedance and is checked against VCTRL-HI to see whether something else drives it.

Besides NTC sensing the pin signals charge done and faults. A 10 kΩ resistor to PGND in place of the NTC disables temperature sensing. Pulling the pin above VCTRL-HI shuts the receiver down with charge complete; pulling it under VCTRL-LOW shuts it down with a fault.
At TJ-SD the LDO turns off; it resumes once the die has cooled by TJ-Hys.

So the transmitter can watch for power lost into foreign objects, the receiver reports received power: its output power plus losses in the coil, resonant capacitor, shielding, rectifier, regulator and metal parts. Certification on a calibrated reference transmitter requires the reported value to sit between 0 and 375 mW below the transmitted power. Transmitters are certified by keeping reference metal objects (a disc, a coin and foil) under 60 °C or 80 °C.

Start-up is the first transfer and handshake; power transfer is any time the two sides communicate and power flows; charge termination covers charge complete as well as removal from the pad, overtemperature and other faults.

C1 (series) and C2 (parallel) form the dual resonant tank with the coil. L's is measured with the coil as built (back cover and battery in place) over a 50 mm × 50 mm × 1 mm TDK PC44 ferrite at a 3.4 mm gap, at 1 V RMS and 100 kHz; Ls is the free-space value. With Ls = 11 µH, L's = 16 µH and 191 mΩ, C1 comes to 158.3 nF (range about 144 nF to 175 nF); 68 nF + 47 nF + 39 nF = 154 nF is used, three parts giving finer values, lower resistance and better heat spread. C2 comes to 2.3 nF, built as 2.2 nF + 100 pF. All are rated 25 V or more; Q comes out above 500.

These usually match the evaluation module. BOOT: 10 nF, at least 10 V. CLAMP: 0.47 µF, 25 V. COMM: 22 nF, 25 V; 47 nF if communication proves weak, at some cost in efficiency, since a larger capacitor swings the coil further.
800 mA needs RILIM = 393 Ω. RFOD starts at 200 Ω before FOD calibration, leaving 205 Ω for R1. An 80 mA termination is 10 % of IBULK, so RTERM = 2.4 kΩ.

AD goes to the external USB supply and AD-EN drives the gate of the blocking FET Q1. EN2, under host control, decides whether the wired source is allowed. With wired power present and allowed, BAT is turned off and Q1 is turned on through AD-EN; an external charger then takes over charging. With no wireless power AD and AD-EN still work, so wired charging goes on.
D1 is a 2.1 V LED at 2 mA with a 100 Ω resistor R4 on the open-drain CHG. RECT uses two 10 µF and one 0.1 µF, 25 V; BAT uses 1.0 µF and 0.1 µF.
Power comes from a Qi-compatible transmitter.

Keep AC1, AC2 and BAT low in resistance. Place the resonant, COMM, CLAMP and BOOT capacitors as close to the part as possible, and high-frequency bypass capacitors close to RECT and the output. Via the PGND net generously for signal integrity and heat. Keep the ILIM and FOD resistor loops to PGND small. Solder the RHL thermal pad to ground. AC1, AC2, BOOT1, BOOT2, COMM1 and COMM2 are the noisy nodes: keep them away from sensing traces, shield them with ground copper beneath, and return every component to a ground plane through vias, two per power-stage capacitor and one per small-signal capacitor.
